questions.stem: A 15 month old unvaccinated girl recently returned from a family visit abroad. She has had 3 days of high fever, a hacking cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. Today a blotchy red rash appeared behind her ears and is spreading to her face. Small white spots are seen on the inside of her cheeks.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a rash spreading from behind the ears is measles.

clues: white spots are seen on the inside of her cheeks
steps.x: The three Cs, Koplik spots and the rash pattern.

elim: Fever for 5 days with cracked lips and hand changes, no Koplik spots.
Rash appears as fever settles, without cough or conjunctivitis.
Mild illness with posterior lymphadenopathy, no Koplik spots.
Sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue after a sore throat.

steps.x: B: Measles. Koplik spots plus cough, coryza and conjunctivitis = measles.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has a 2 day history of fever, sore throat and vomiting. He has a rough, sandpaper-like red rash over his chest and abdomen, flushed cheeks with pallor around the mouth, and a bright red tongue with prominent papillae. His tonsils are enlarged with exudate.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sore throat, sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue indicate scarlet fever from Streptococcus pyogenes.

clues: bright red tongue with prominent papillae
steps.x: Sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue.

elim: Slapped cheeks then a lacy rash, no sore throat or strawberry tongue.
Vesicles on palms, soles and mouth.
Needs 5 days of fever with conjunctivitis and extremity changes.
Cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots.

steps.x: E: Scarlet fever. Sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue = scarlet fever.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy at nursery has a 1 day history of low-grade fever and sore mouth. He has small painful ulcers on his tongue and inner cheeks, and oval vesicles surrounded by a red halo on his palms and soles. Several children at nursery have had similar symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Vesicles with an erythematous halo on palms, soles and mouth is hand, foot and mouth disease, caused by Coxsackievirus A16.

steps.x: Mouth ulcers plus palm and sole vesicles.

elim: Causes gingivostomatitis without palm and sole vesicles.
Causes roseola infantum.
Causes slapped cheek syndrome.
Vesicles mainly on the trunk and face.

steps.x: A: Coxsackievirus A16. Hand, foot and mouth = Coxsackievirus A16.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman returned from Thailand 5 days ago. She has a high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes and muscle and joint pains. Today she has a widespread red rash with small scattered islands of normal pale skin within it.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Travel to South-East Asia, fever, retro-orbital pain and a 'white islands in a sea of red' rash is dengue.

steps.x: Travel, retro-orbital pain, a characteristic rash.

elim: Causes fever and rigors without this rash.
Prodrome of cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots.
Sandpaper rash with sore throat in children.
Rose spots on the trunk, abdominal pain and constipation.

steps.x: A: Dengue fever. 'White islands in a sea of red' = dengue fever.

questions.stem: A 5 year old girl has had a mild fever for a day. She now has an itchy rash of red spots on her trunk and face that progress to clear blisters and then cloudy pustules. Her brother had a similar illness 2 weeks ago.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Generalised vesicles evolving into pustules, mainly on the trunk and face, with an infected contact, is chickenpox.

clues: clear blisters and then cloudy pustules
Her brother had a similar illness
steps.x: A vesicular rash with a sibling contact.

elim: Clustered punched-out erosions on existing eczema.
Slapped cheeks and a lacy rash, not vesicles.
Golden crusts, often around the mouth, without fever.
A maculopapular rash as fever settles in an infant.

steps.x: A: Chickenpox. Vesicles to pustules on torso and face = chickenpox.

questions.stem: A 10 month old boy had 3 days of high fever up to 39.8°C but was otherwise fairly well. On the fourth day the fever settled and a pink maculopapular rash appeared on his trunk. He is now happy and feeding well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative virus?
questions.e: Three days of high fever in an infant with a rash appearing as the fever settles is roseola infantum, caused by HHV-6.

clues: the fever settled and a pink maculopapular rash appeared
steps.x: Fever first, rash as it settles, infant age.

elim: Causes hand, foot and mouth disease.
Rash appears with high fever after cough, coryza and conjunctivitis.
Slapped cheeks then a lacy rash.
Mild fever with lymphadenopathy and a rash at the same time.

steps.x: B: Human herpesvirus 6. Roseola = HHV-6: fever for 3 days, rash on day 4.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has bright red cheeks, as if he has been slapped, after a week of mild cold symptoms. Two days later a lacy, net-like rash appears on his arms and trunk. He is now well and afebrile.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Slapped cheek rash followed by a lacy reticular rash on the limbs is erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19).

clues: as if he has been slapped
steps.x: Slapped cheeks then a lacy rash.

elim: Unilateral, painful and hot, with fever.
A pink rash spreading from the face with lymphadenopathy.
Flushed cheeks with sore throat and sandpaper rash.
A malar rash in older patients with joint pains.

steps.x: B: Erythema infectiosum. Slapped cheeks then a lacy limb rash = fifth disease (parvovirus B19).

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman who missed her childhood vaccinations had a mild illness 1 week ago with low-grade fever, enlarged lymph nodes behind her ears and a pink rash that started on her face and spread down her body. She now has painful swelling of the small joints of both hands.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her joint symptoms?
questions.e: Rubella causes arthritis of the small joints, especially in adult women.

steps.x: A rubella-like illness followed by small joint arthritis.

elim: Usually a single joint, often the big toe, after no viral illness.
Affects older people with gradual onset.
Affects large lower limb joints after diarrhoea.
A single hot joint with high fever.

steps.x: D: Rubella arthritis. Rubella complication: arthritis of small joints.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy who was not vaccinated had painful swelling in front of both ears and fever 5 days ago. He now has a painful, swollen right testis with fever. Urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Mumps causes parotitis and can be complicated by orchitis and deafness.

clues: swelling in front of both ears
steps.x: Parotitis then testicular swelling.

elim: Usually with urinary symptoms and positive dipstick.
A groin lump, not a tender testis after parotitis.
A painless lump.
Sudden severe pain, no preceding parotitis.

steps.x: C: Mumps orchitis. Mumps complications: orchitis, deafness.

questions.stem: An 18 month old girl has had a high fever of 40°C for 2 days. While her temperature is at its peak she has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes, then recovers fully. On day 4 her fever settles and a pink rash appears on her trunk.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the seizure?
questions.e: Roseola infantum causes febrile convulsions in 10 to 15% of children.

clues: pink rash appears on her trunk
steps.x: High fever, brief seizure, rash as fever settles.

elim: She recovered fully and later developed the typical roseola rash.
A single seizure with high fever in a toddler is a febrile convulsion.
No suggestion of poor feeding or diabetes.
Measles has a prodrome with Koplik spots.

steps.x: C: Febrile convulsion from roseola infantum. Roseola: febrile convulsions in 10-15%.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy has had chickenpox for 4 days and has been given ibuprofen for fever. He now has severe pain and a rapidly spreading area of dusky redness on his thigh. His temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 168 bpm and capillary refill 4 seconds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Chickenpox, especially with NSAIDs, is a risk factor for necrotising fasciitis.

clues: rapidly spreading area of dusky redness
steps.x: Chickenpox, NSAIDs, rapid spread and shock.

elim: Pain would match the skin and he would not be shocked.
Target lesions without severe pain or shock.
Palpable purpura on the legs without sepsis.
Causes ataxia or confusion, not a spreading limb infection.

steps.x: D: Necrotising fasciitis. Chickenpox plus NSAIDs raises necrotising fasciitis risk.

questions.stem: A 2 year old unvaccinated boy has had measles for 6 days. His rash is fading, but he now has a temperature of 39.5°C, a productive cough, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. There are crackles at the right base.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Pneumonia is the most common cause of death in measles.

steps.x: Hypoxia, fever and focal crackles after measles.

elim: The most common complication, but would cause ear pain, not hypoxia and crackles.
Wheeze without fever and focal crackles.
Affects infants under 1 with RSV.
A late neurological complication years later.

steps.x: D: Pneumonia. Measles: otitis media most common, pneumonia the commonest cause of death.

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl has had 2 days of fever, runny nose and malaise. Today a widespread blanching maculopapular rash appeared, starting on her face and trunk. She has no conjunctivitis, no mouth lesions, no vesicles and no sore throat. She is alert and drinking well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever and URTI symptoms followed by a widespread blanching maculopapular rash in a well child is a viral exanthem.

steps.x: Viral prodrome, then a blanching rash, child well.

elim: No new medication.
Non-blanching purpura in an unwell child.
Needs sore throat and a sandpaper rash.
Itchy wheals that come and go, no viral prodrome.

steps.x: C: Non-specific viral exanthem. Fever then maculopapular rash on face or trunk in a child = viral exanthem.

questions.stem: A 2 year old boy has 3 days of fever followed by a pink rash as the fever settled. He is alert, playing and drinking well. His mother asks whether he needs any tests.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Viral exanthems are diagnosed clinically from fever, rash and associated features.

steps.x: A classic roseola picture in a well child.

elim: He is well.
Does not change management.
No meningism; he is well.
Only if severe.

steps.x: B: Clinical diagnosis without tests. Viral exanthem = clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 14 month old unvaccinated boy with a febrile rash is admitted with hypoxia and bilateral crackles. Measles is suspected but he has no Koplik spots and the rash is atypical. Public health needs confirmation of the organism.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the cause?
questions.e: In severe cases, blood tests and viral PCR confirm the causative organism.

clues: Public health needs confirmation of the organism
steps.x: A severe illness needing the organism confirmed.

elim: Does not identify the virus.
Shows pneumonia but not the virus.
Tests for EBV.
Detects streptococci, not measles.

steps.x: E: Viral PCR. If severe: viral PCR to confirm the cause.

questions.stem: A 2 year old girl has a mild fever, sore mouth and red-rimmed vesicles on her palms and soles. Her nursery has had several similar cases this week. She is drinking small amounts but has wet nappies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Hand, foot and mouth disease is a clinical diagnosis that resolves in 7 to 10 days.

clues: red-rimmed vesicles on her palms and soles
steps.x: A typical picture in a hydrated child.

elim: Not needed in a well child.
Does not alter management.
Not needed in a clear clinical picture.
Only if severe.

steps.x: C: No investigation needed. Clinical diagnosis; PCR only if severe.

questions.stem: An 8 year old boy with sickle cell disease is pale and breathless 1 week after a classmate had slapped cheek syndrome. His haemoglobin is 48 g/L, down from his usual 85 g/L. The team wants to confirm the cause.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the organism?
questions.e: In severe disease such as aplastic crisis, viral PCR confirms the organism.

steps.x: Sickle cell, sudden anaemia, parvovirus contact.

elim: Detect bacteria, not parvovirus.
Tests for immune haemolysis.
Confirms sickle cell, already known.
Not relevant.

steps.x: D: Parvovirus B19 PCR. Severe exanthem: confirm with viral PCR.

questions.stem: A 5 year old girl has a 1 day history of sore throat and fever, and a sandpaper rash on her trunk with a strawberry tongue. Her GP diagnoses scarlet fever.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate basis for the diagnosis?
questions.e: Exanthems including scarlet fever are diagnosed clinically from fever, rash and features such as strawberry tongue.

steps.x: A classic picture.

elim: Rises weeks later.
Not needed.
Not needed.
Scarlet fever is bacterial and clinical.

steps.x: C: Clinical features alone. Clinical diagnosis based on fever, rash and associated features.

questions.stem: A 2 year old boy has a 2 day history of fever, runny nose and a widespread blanching maculopapular rash. He is alert, drinking well and passing urine. His temperature is 38.3°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Viral exanthem management is supportive: paracetamol, fluids and rest.

steps.x: A well child with a viral rash.

elim: He is well; no suspicion of sepsis.
No indication.
Viral illness; no bacterial cause.
No indication.

steps.x: E: Paracetamol, fluids and rest. Supportive: paracetamol, hydration, rest.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl with chickenpox is very itchy and cannot sleep despite calamine lotion. She is otherwise well and afebrile.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: Itch in viral exanthems is treated with oral antihistamines such as chlorphenamine.

steps.x: Itch is the problem.

elim: NSAIDs increase necrotising fasciitis risk in chickenpox.
Not routine in healthy children.
No bacterial infection.
Not used for chickenpox itch.

steps.x: C: Oral chlorphenamine. Itch: oral antihistamine (chlorphenamine).

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy is diagnosed with scarlet fever. He has no penicillin allergy. His father asks when he can go back to school.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management and advice?
o: Amoxicillin; return when the rash fades
No antibiotics; return when fever settles
questions.e: Scarlet fever is treated with phenoxymethylpenicillin and children may return 24 hours after starting.

steps.x: Scarlet fever, needs antibiotic and exclusion advice.

elim: Not first-line and wrong exclusion.
Used in penicillin allergy.
Scarlet fever needs antibiotics.
Return is 24 hours after starting.

steps.x: D: Phenoxymethylpenicillin; return 24 hours after starting. Scarlet fever: phenoxymethylpenicillin; school after 24 hours of antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl has hand, foot and mouth disease. She is drinking well. Her mother asks how long it will last and whether her baby brother might catch it.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Resolves in 24 hours; spread by mosquitoes
Resolves in 6 weeks; spread only by touch
Resolves in 7 to 10 days; spread by faecal-oral and droplets
questions.e: Hand, foot and mouth is self-limiting, resolving in 7 to 10 days, and spreads by faecal-oral and respiratory droplets.

steps.x: Asking about course and spread.

elim: Not the course or route.
Symptomatic only and contagious.
Wrong course and route.
Wrong course; also faecal-oral.

steps.x: E: Resolves in 7 to 10 days; spread by faecal-oral and droplets. HFM: symptomatic only, 7-10 days, faecal-oral and droplet spread.

questions.stem: A 5 year old boy has chickenpox. He is well. His mother has been giving him ibuprofen and wants to send him back to school tomorrow, although some vesicles are still not crusted.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop ibuprofen; exclude until all lesions crust
questions.e: Avoid NSAIDs in chickenpox and exclude from school until all lesions have crusted.

clues: some vesicles are still not crusted
steps.x: NSAIDs and uncrusted lesions.

elim: NSAIDs and early return are both wrong.
Not routine and wrong exclusion.
Not bacterial.
He is still infectious.

steps.x: D: Stop ibuprofen; exclude until all lesions crust. Chickenpox: calamine and paracetamol, no NSAIDs, exclude until crusted.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl with chickenpox has several lesions on her face that have become crusted with honey-coloured material and surrounding redness. She is well and afebrile with no penicillin allergy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Secondary bacterial infection of an exanthem is treated with flucloxacillin.

steps.x: Secondary bacterial skin infection.

elim: Treats VZV, not the bacterial infection.
For itch only.
An antifungal.
Treats scarlet fever, not staphylococcal skin infection.

steps.x: D: Flucloxacillin. Secondary bacterial infection: flucloxacillin.

questions.stem: A 5 year old girl has scarlet fever after a streptococcal sore throat. The rash is widespread, although bacteria are only present in her throat. A student asks how the infection causes the rash.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: Scarlet fever rash is toxin-mediated by streptococcal erythrogenic exotoxin.

steps.x: A rash distant from the infection.

elim: Bacteria are only in the throat.
Not the mechanism of scarlet fever.
Not an IgE response.
Scarlet fever is bacterial.

steps.x: C: Streptococcal erythrogenic exotoxin. Scarlet fever is toxin-mediated (erythrogenic exotoxin).

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl recovering from measles develops a purulent ear discharge and bacterial pneumonia within the same week. Her parents ask why measles made her catch other infections.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Measles directly invades the middle ear
questions.e: Measles causes transient immune suppression, predisposing to secondary bacterial infections such as otitis media and pneumonia.

clues: purulent ear discharge and bacterial pneumonia
steps.x: Several bacterial infections after measles.

elim: Not the mechanism described.
The secondary infections are bacterial.
She had natural infection.
Not true.

steps.x: B: Measles causes transient immune suppression. Measles: transient immunosuppression causes secondary bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A 12 year old girl with hereditary spherocytosis becomes pale and tired 10 days after her cousin had slapped cheeks. Her reticulocyte count is very low. A student asks why this virus causes such severe anaemia in her.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Infection of erythroid progenitors when red cell turnover is high
Viral haemolysis of mature red cells
questions.e: Parvovirus B19 targets erythroid progenitor cells, so people with chronic haemolysis develop aplastic crisis.

steps.x: Chronic haemolysis plus marrow failure after parvovirus.

elim: This is ITP.
Not caused by parvovirus.
Not the mechanism.
The reticulocyte count is low, showing marrow failure.

steps.x: C: Infection of erythroid progenitors when red cell turnover is high. Parvovirus B19 -> erythroid progenitors -> aplastic crisis in haemolytic anaemias.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman who is 8 weeks pregnant develops a pink rash and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy. She was not vaccinated. Rubella is confirmed. She asks why the infection is dangerous for her baby.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Rubella crosses the placenta and disrupts organogenesis
Rubella is dangerous only in the third trimester
questions.e: Rubella crosses the placenta and disrupts organogenesis, especially in the first trimester (congenital rubella syndrome).

steps.x: First-trimester rubella.

elim: Not the main risk.
Not the mechanism.
That is parvovirus.
First trimester is the most dangerous.

steps.x: D: Rubella crosses the placenta and disrupts organogenesis. Rubella in the first trimester -> congenital rubella syndrome.

questions.stem: A 16 month old boy had 3 days of high fever and now has a pink rash on his trunk as the fever has settled. His nursery asks whether he must stay at home now that the rash has appeared.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for why exclusion is not needed?
o: Rash appears after the infectious period
Roseola is spread only by blood
The rash is caused by a toxin
questions.e: In roseola and erythema infectiosum the rash appears after the infectious viraemic period.

steps.x: Rash appears after fever resolves.

elim: There is no roseola vaccine.
Not the reason.
It affects infants.
Not the reason.

steps.x: B: Rash appears after the infectious period. Roseola and fifth disease: rash after the infectious period.

questions.stem: A nursery has an outbreak of hand, foot and mouth disease among 2 and 3 year olds. The manager asks how it spreads and why the spots appear in the mouth and on hands and feet.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate explanation?
o: Faecal-oral and droplet spread, replicating in gut and skin epithelium
Insect bites, replicating in lymph nodes
questions.e: Coxsackievirus spreads faecal-orally and by droplets and replicates in gut and skin/mucosal epithelium.

clues: outbreak of hand, foot and mouth disease
steps.x: A nursery outbreak.

elim: Not the route.
Describes arboviruses.
Describes herpes simplex.
Not the route.

steps.x: B: Faecal-oral and droplet spread, replicating in gut and skin epithelium. HFM: faecal-oral and droplet; replicates in gut and skin epithelium.
